title: Chapter 13: Tuples and Sets: Fixed Groups and Unique Items
video_title: Python Chapter 13: Tuples and Sets, Fixed Groups and Unique Items
summary: Omar is in Asha's customer list four times, so a list counts visits, not people. Follow Asha as she learns tuples and sets: fixed groups, unpacking and swapping, lists of tuples, removing repeats, add and discard, and comparing two days of customers. Then watch her build a welcome with an AI assistant at all six stages. She asks for trade-offs, and catches empty curly brackets, a wrong prediction, and a change that removed every welcome.

visual.heading: Why this matters
visual.label: The big picture
items: A **set** keeps each item only once. It counts people, not visits.
A **tuple** keeps a fixed group, such as the opening hours.
A booking site keeps each seat once. A map stores each place as a fixed pair of numbers.

segments.say: A set keeps each item only once, so it counts people, not visits. A tuple keeps a fixed group together, such as the opening hours.
A booking site keeps each seat once. A map stores each place as a fixed pair of numbers. The right collection makes code shorter and safer.

scenes.title: The idea: four collections
scenes.direction: Teach the four collections with the table, row by row, then the bag of name cards. Then a quiz and a breather.

segments.say: You now know four collections. A list, in square brackets, keeps order, allows repeats, and can change.
A tuple, in round brackets, is like a list that cannot change.
A set uses curly brackets with values inside. It keeps no order, and each item appears only once.
And a dictionary also uses curly brackets, but with keys and values. Each key appears once.

visual.heading: A set is like a bag of name cards
visual.label: Analogy
items: Each name card is in the bag once. The cards are in no fixed order.
Unlike a bag: a set ignores a card that is already inside.
Add Omar four times, and the set still holds one Omar.

segments.say: Think of a set as a bag of name cards, in no fixed order. Unlike a real bag, a set ignores a card that is already inside. Add Omar four times, and it still holds one Omar.

visual.question: Which collection keeps each item only once, in no fixed order?
visual.explain: A set keeps each item once and has no order.

segments.say: Quick check. Which collection keeps each item only once, in no fixed order?

after.say: D. A set. Each item once, and no fixed order.

items: A list keeps every repeat.
A tuple is a fixed group.
A set keeps each item once.

scenes.title: Step 4: Remove repeats with a set

segments.say: Step 4. Line 2 lists five visits, with Omar three times. Line 3 turns the list into a set, and every repeat disappears.
A set has no order, so it has no positions, and printed directly, its names can change order between runs. So line 6 prints sorted, a list in a fixed order.
And in checks a set quickly, even when it holds thousands of names.

after.say: 5, then 3. The list has five visits, but the set has three different customers.
Line 6 shows them in order: Lina, Omar, Sam. Lina is in the set, and Ravi is not.

visual.heading: Step 5: add() and discard()

segments.say: Step 5. Line 2 makes an empty set, with set and round brackets.
Add puts an item into the set. Lines 3 to 5 add Omar, Lina, and Omar again. Remember the bag of name cards.
Line 6 prints the sorted names and the number of items.

after.say: Lina and Omar, and 2. The second Omar changed nothing: he was already inside.
Discard takes an item out. Line 8 discards Zoe, who is not in the set, and there is no error.
And line 10 shows an important rule. Empty curly brackets make an empty dictionary. To make an empty set, write set, with round brackets.

visual.question: How do you make an empty set?
visual.explain: `{}` makes an empty dictionary. `set()` makes an empty set.

segments.say: Quick check. How do you make an empty set?

scenes.title: Step 6: Compare two sets
scenes.direction: Teach the four operators with the table, then the code. Ask what line 6 prints, then reveal all four.

visual.heading: Step 6: Four ways to compare two sets
visual.label: Build it

segments.say: Step 6. Four operators compare two sets. The bar is union: items in either set.
The and sign is intersection: items in both.
Minus is difference: items in the first set only.
And the hat sign is symmetric difference: items in one set, but not both.

visual.heading: Step 6: Today and yesterday
visual.hidden_text: Predict the output before it appears.

segments.say: Today, Omar, Lina and Sam came in. Yesterday, Lina, Ravi and Sam.
Line 6 takes yesterday away from today.

after.say: Omar, only. He came today, but not yesterday.
Union gives all four names, and intersection gives Lina and Sam, who came both days.
Symmetric difference gives Omar and Ravi: each came on one day only. And for minus, the order matters. Yesterday minus today would give Ravi.

visual.heading: This chapter's AI skill: ask for trade-offs
visual.label: Before you start
items: "Which is best?" gets one answer you cannot judge.
"Compare the options, with a strength and a weakness each" gets an answer you can check.
Never paste private data. You are responsible for the code you use.

segments.say: This chapter's AI skill is asking for trade-offs: what you gain and what you lose with each choice. Ask for a strength and a weakness for each option, and you get an answer you can check.

messages.text: I want to welcome each customer the first time they come in today, in the order they arrive. Compare a list, a tuple, a set and a dictionary for remembering who I have welcomed. One strength and one weakness each. Do not choose for me.

List: keeps order. Weakness: `in` checks every item, one by one.
Tuple: fixed. Weakness: you cannot add a name.
Set: each name once, and `in` is fast. Weakness: no order.
Dictionary: can count visits per name. Weakness: more than you need.

segments.say: Stage 1: plan. Asha wants to welcome each customer the first time they come in, in the order they arrive. She asks the AI to compare all four collections, and not to choose for her.
The AI gives a strength and a weakness for each. Asha chooses: the visit list keeps the order, and a set remembers who she has already welcomed.

The AI predicts each case. For case 3, Omar and omar with a space, it predicts one welcome for Omar.

segments.say: Asha runs every case. The normal day: Omar, Lina and Sam are welcomed once each. New today, 3. Pass.
The empty day: no welcomes, and New today, 0. Pass.

visual.label: Test

visual.heading: Debug: the cause before the fix

segments.say: Stage 5: debug. Asha cleans each name on line 5, with strip and title from Chapter 3. But she types line 8 too fast, and the program stops. She pastes the code and the full error, and asks for the cause first.

messages.text: What is the cause, and the smallest fix?

Line 8 uses square brackets after `add`. `add` is a method, so you call it with round brackets: `seen.add(name)`.
"Not subscriptable" means you cannot use square brackets on it.

segments.say: The AI names line 8: square brackets after add. Add is a method, so it needs round brackets. Not subscriptable means you cannot use square brackets on it.
A fix can break a case that worked before, so Asha runs all three cases again. Lines 2 to 4 keep each case name with its list of visits.
Line 9 cleans each name, and line 12 now uses round brackets.
The normal day: three welcomes, New today 3. Pass.
Omar typed two ways: one welcome for Omar, then Lina. New today, 2. Pass.
And the empty day: New today, 0. Pass. All three cases pass.

messages.text: My program passes every case. Suggest one change that makes it shorter, with one reason. The output must stay exactly the same.
Make the set from the list on line 3: `seen = set(today)`. The set then holds every name already, so you can delete the `add` line. The output stays the same.

segments.say: Stage 6: improve. Asha asks for one change that makes the code shorter. And she adds: the output must stay exactly the same.
The AI suggests making the set from the whole list on line 3. Then the add line is not needed, it says.

scenes.title: Common mistakes
scenes.direction: Mistake 1 shows changing a tuple. Mistakes 2 and 3 are spot-it questions on rules taught in steps 1 and 4. The video leaves the unpacking mistake to the lesson.

segments.say: Mistake 1. Line 3 prints the hours. Line 4 tries to change the opening hour to 9.
A tuple cannot change, so Python stops with a Type Error. Does not support item assignment means you cannot give one position a new value.
The fix: make a new tuple, nine and eighteen. Or use a list if the values change often.

visual.hidden_text: Find the problem before the answer appears.

after.say: There is no error, which makes this mistake hard to see. The fix: a comma after the value, as on line 4.

scenes.title: Recap
scenes.direction: Each recap point appears as it is spoken, then a final quick check, then the badge.

visual.heading: Recap
visual.label: What you learned
items: A tuple is a fixed group in round brackets. Read it like a list; you cannot change it.
Unpacking puts each value into its own variable: `opens, closes = hours`.
A set keeps each item once and has no order. `set(visits)` removes repeats.
`{}` is an empty dictionary. An empty set is `set()`.
`|`, `&`, `-` and `^` compare two sets. Print `sorted(...)` for a fixed order.
Ask AI to compare options with trade-offs, then choose and test.

segments.say: Let's recap. A tuple is a fixed group you cannot change, and unpacking puts each value into its own variable.
A set keeps each item once, with no order. An empty set is set, with round brackets.
Four operators compare two sets, and sorted gives a fixed order.
And with AI: ask for trade-offs, then choose and test yourself.

visual.question: `a = {"tea", "cake"}` and `b = {"cake", "scone"}`. What does `sorted(a & b)` give?
visual.explain: `&` gives the items in both sets. Only cake is in both.

segments.say: One last check. Set a holds tea and cake. Set b holds cake and scone. What does sorted of a and b give, with the and sign?

after.say: C. Cake, only. The and sign gives the items in both sets.
